As we enter a new year, I will put out the call again for new
Vampire: Elder Kindred Network Newsletter Writers.
We had 6 clans represented in October, 8 in November,
but only 6 again in December. To see an archive of newsletters, go
to:

http://www.thelasombra.com/ClanPages/

If your favorite clan does not currently have a newsletter being
written, or if it has never had a newsletter written for it,
consider becoming an editor/creator/writer. To see the newsletters
archived by month, go here:

http://www.thelasombra.com/newsletter.htm

Frequently Asked Questions about the Clan Newsletters:

Q) What content can be included in a V:EKN Clan Newsletter?
A) Just about anything on the topic of your clan or the game.
Some of the things that have been included
in past newsletters include:
-Vampire fiction
-Deck designs
-Clan strategy
-Discipline overviews
-Library Card overviews
-Crypt Card overviews

Q) What has to be included in a V:EKN Clan Newsletter?
A) You are free to write anything you want about your clan
of choice, as long as it is interesting and entertaining.
As official representitives of V:TES, however, you should
keep your Newsletters intelligent, on topic, and in support
of the official rules (i.e. no Newsletter tirades regarding
how you hate errata or how you think the game is best played
with a one card limit). Variant rules and ideas are fine,
but please keep in mind that you are a representitive of
the V:TES community as a whole.

Q) How should I publish my Clan newsletter?
A) Post your Newsletters to the Usenet newsgroup
rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad. As the Clan Newsletters
are primarily a function of usenet, please always post
your Newsletter on rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad (the
official V:TES newsgroup). Alternately, you can post
them to the White Wolf Forums, and they will be transferred
to the newsgroup for you. Some folks post their newsletters
on personal web pages, and there are some unofficial web
sites that archive Clan Newsletters, but these are run and
managed privately -- the VEKN takes no responsibility in
archiving or posting Clan Newsletters on the web.

Q) How often should I publish a Clan newsletter?
A) As often as you are inspired. If a newsletter
goes into a remission of 3 months, new editors will be
solicited.

Q) Is there any sort of renumeration available as a Newsletter Editor?
A) Only the respect and admiration of your peers.

Q) Who do I ask questions of about becoming a newsletter editor
or about my newsletter before I publish it?
A) Direct questions about clan reservations to Peter Bakija,
and you may also ask questions of him or of the other newsletter
editors if you want to clarify a rules situation or card combo
before publishing. [www.myplanet.net/pdb6/vtes.html]

Q) Isn't this FAQ self-important, self-righteous and obnoxious?
A) No, only the FAQ Compiler is self-righteous and obnoxious.

Q) Does the FAQ Compiler have anything to do with producing these
newsletters?
A) Not in the slightest. Currently, I archive, and nothing more.

Q) If I don't care to pay too much attention to the newsgroup, can
I sign up somewhere to have the VEKN Newsletters emailed to me?
A) Yes. You can access it here:

http://groups.yahoo.com/group/VTES-Newsletters

The official word follows:

http://www.myplanet.net/pdb6/newsleters.html
http://www.myplanet.net/pdb6/veknfaq.html

So you want to write a VTES Clan newsletter? Here is what is involved:

A) Pick a clan. Many clans are already claimed, although most folks
(including me) have been slacking off of late. Anyway, pick one you
like, and e-mail me to see if it available.

B) Write Newsletters. The content can be anything you want. Some
suggestions:
-Vampire fiction
-Deck designs
-Clan strategy
-Discipline overviews
-Card overviews

You are free to write anything you want about your clan of choice, as
long as it is interesting and entertaining. As official
representitives of VTES, however, you should keep your Newsletters
intelligent, on topic, and in support of the official rules (i.e. no
Newsletter tirades regarding how you hate errata or how you think the
game is best played with a one card limit). Variant rules and ideas
are fine, but please keep in mind that you are a representitive of the
VTES community as a whole.

C) Post your Newsletters. As the Clan Newsletters are primarily a
function of usenet, please always post your Newsletter on
rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad (the official VTES newsgroup). How often
you post them is up to you. The original plan was to post a new one
every month, but after four years, things get slack.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
The Lasombra wrote:

> If your favorite clan does not currently have a newsletter being
> written, or if it has never had a newsletter written for it,
> consider becoming an editor/creator/writer.

Those of you out there writing newsletters, or checking to see if there is a
newsletter taken, or checking to see if you are a newlsetter writer of a
particular clan:

There is a list of "active" newsletter writers somewhere (my web site? the
FAQ?), and while it exists, it is mostly wrong, if not completely
irrelevant. While a small handfull of folks are fairly consistient with
wirting newsletters, most people who get involved do so for a short period
of time, usually writing one or two newsletters and then moving on--this
isn't a bad thing (it is better for folks to write something once or twice
than to never write anything at all), but makes keeping track of who is
writing what very difficult, to the point that I completely game up even
trying at some point.

Feel free to drop me a line if you are interested in a particular clan, but
in reality, the best thing to do is to check out the Lasombra's archives,
see if a particular clan has had a newsletter in the last 3 or 4 months, and
if not, feel free to write one. In the best situation, you are going to post
something interesting and fun to read. In the worst situation, you are going
to post something interesting to read that will be redundant with something
someone else writes (but if a newsletter hasn't been published for a
multitude of months, it seems unlikely that one will show up at the same
time as a new one).

If someone does post a newsletter for a clan that you already "own", and
this is problematic, send me an e-mail, and I'm sure we can work something
out.

The Most Active newsletters of late have been:

!Gangrel (4 in last 4 months)
Toreador (4 in last 4 months)
Nosferatu/!Nosferatu (3 in last 4 months)
Brujah (3 in last 4 months)
Ahrimanes (2 in last 4 months)
!Toreador (2 in last 4 months)

And then a bunch of clans that have been published once in the last 4
months. Assume that if a newsletter has been published in the last 4 months,
that clan is "taken"--if you still want to write for it, drop an e-mail to
the author and see if you can work something out.

Regardless, if you are interested in writing a newsletter for posting on
this newsgroup, archiving on a web site and/or distributing through the
newsletter list serve, check out the FAQ (on my or the Lasombra's web site),
read some old newsletters, write something interesting, and post away.

I have another issue of the Picayune to publish, and as Editor I'd be a
lot more motivated getting them out on schedule if more feedback were
given.
It's like a roommate of mine from college that we'd always asked if he
wanted to join us for "x" activity, and then bitched when we stopped
asking (because he always declined joining us in the past).

The Path of Blood and Necromancing the Bones sites are probably a better

http://www.wizkidsgames.com/

Makes me wonder who heads up Marketing strategy at WW?

active for so long, it's like they adopted the strategy of "Why buy the
cow if you're getting the milk for free?".

Their website has a problem dealing with firewall software as well.
It's a real treat having to disable my firewall to access their forums
or generate a list of players/princes.

Well, it seems like the cow's dried up, ain't no corn in the field, the
chicken is only laying an egg a day, and the bank is about to foreclose
on the farm.

point where everyone could gather. There are some good sites out there
(RustWurk, Lasombra's, VEKN Texas, etc..) not one has really become a
national hotspot for VTES collaboration and gathering.

The existing long-term playerbase is faltering as the old-timers are
moving on to other things, and not much influx of new players to speak
of. At least from what I've seen in Michigan and on the NG.
Perhaps my worldview on this may/may not accurately reflect other folks
areas, but that's how it feels to me regardless.

There are so many ways that WW could persue expanding their CCG
playerbase, if they wanted to invest the effort (and in some cases,
money).

Okay, I'm done griping for today :-P

I now return you back to the regular NewsGroup threads, all 6 or 7 of
them..

Messages.Body:
In message <20030103115040...@mb-cg.aol.com>, Curevei

<cur...@aol.commetal> writes:
>I would point out that a well supported CCG has expansions at least every 6
>months.

Why?

A CCG could have expansions released every 6 months. But it could then
also sacrifice card quality (in terms of design, balance). Or it could
sacrifice any attempt at rules consistency. And if you're talking at
least every six months, what are we doing? 3 a year? 4 a year?

Assume that the V:TES expansions were being done every 6 months.
Playtesting and such like generally takes several months, then that has
to be fed back into the design process at the end, then final editing.
If you're doing those every three months, or every four months, there's
a lot of overlap. Would it be fair for people to playtest The Camarilla
Edition without even knowing what's in Bloodlines, or vaguely how it
works? Is that "well supported"?

Speed of production doesn't mean it's well supported. On the contrary,
it could be just as indicative of an exploitative company with a cash
cow mentality. Screw the players, up the power levels, twist the thumb
screws. Good for a short burst of publicity, cash and interest. For
the long haul, not a good idea. For a company which has a reputation of
giving a shit about its products and its players, also quite likely not
a good idea.

(For example, White Wolf had a fair amount of demand for a Mage Mind's
Eye Theatre set, but didn't release one until they had one they were
*happy* with. That's a very different business ethos to one which drops
products out left, right and centre on the premise that people will keep
buying them.)

>The reason for such support is to hold certain people's interest. Not
>everyone is a diehard. Lot of fickle CCGers.

This is different from an arbitrary definition of a well-supported CCG.

What this is is a CCG that has identified a 'niche' market of people who
will buy lots of cards, but only if there's a continual chase for new
cards. Magic, Pokémon and Harry Potter each identify well with a young
market - look around at a Magic convention tournament, and the average
age is much less than that of V:TES.

And try to identify any card games *outside* of the obvious
Hasbro/Wizards set that release at least every six months that have any
longevity. I'd struggle to name many.

So V:TES plays to a different brand of players. Why bother competing in
the hugely overcrowded 14yo's who won't care about your game without a
truck of marketing when your other markets are ticking over very nicely?
And why piss off your other markets when it's a very risky business
trying to take on Hasbro head to head over huge media extravaganza card
games? Very easy to get burned.

>I don't see how an expansion
>every 9 months does anything to expand the player base; just caters to the
>existing "I have tons of cards and lots of ideas I haven't gotten around to"
>crowd.

What's three months? People who are so fickle that three months is
sufficient to drop them from the game are possibly going to drop it
*anyway*. And how many of the existing player base are you going to
push away by dropping three expansions a year? Lots of people *don't*
play Magic or Star Trek and similar, because they don't like the games
that force you to shit money. And without the existing player base, how
are you going to expand the game? Who's going to give the demos, when
the game's dead? And who's going to buy a game when everyone they know
who plays it has just quit?

Also, bear in mind that V:TES expansions recently have been rather
large. Bloodlines was a small expansion, yet also a huge one at the
same time. The fallback levels of cards mean that some cards are two
different cards - some of the fallback levels are *really* good. And
the extra nuance of the dual-discipline cards and so forth is extra
tricky. It's certainly more cards than the actual numbers say, if you
see what I mean.

These aren't small expansions. There's a lot of cards to buy. If you
want it split up into two lots of 100, there's not a lot of difference.
Sure, you get a new box on the shelf - but at the same time, you create
another problem for retailers of "Do I buy this one or this one?" and
more headaches with printing and distributing. Even if you print two
expansions at once, we've already seen the trouble that some printers
give in terms of card separation - how do you cope when instead of three
cards dropping into a handful of boosters (Xavier, Wind Dance, Eye of
Hazimel) it's actually 100 cards dropping into a lot more? You're still
not someone with the might of Hasbro to spank printers, you're working
with far smaller numbers.

>I really don't want to dwell on this too much, but I'm eager for an expansion.
>I don't subscribe to the theory that a set has to be played until it's stale
>which is what I see as the natural result of examining a set "completely" or
>whatever word people have been using.

There's a difference between "stale" and actually getting to look at a
set and use it a bit. Each V:TES set so far under White Wolf has been
very different from the last. This isn't Magic where the whole year is
themed on Weatherlight or Ice Age or somesuch, and so you can just pick
up brand new cards and they're just like the last lot.

Sabbat War was a straight reprint for much of it, with some additions.
Final Nights introduced a slew of new cards. Bloodlines was one of the
kookiest expansions (in a good way) ever released for a CCG that I've
come across. (Magic Unglued does not count. Kooky in a useful way.)
The Camarilla Edition introduced some serious new mechanics (Grouping).
Drop those in two or three times a year and who can keep up?

A "well supported" game definition such as "at least every six months
for expansions" takes the quality of the cards out of the definition.

If expansions are being dropped every four months, a great deal of time
and effort is needed to thoroughly playtest these things.

This splits off into two distinct areas. Either you playtest, say,
Final Nights as a whole, and then release it 'Magic style' (possibly
closer to some of the Five Rings Publishing storyline boxes) with a
themed set over the year, or you're still releasing the same number of
cards.

In the former instance, cost is upped (fewer economies of scale) or the
whole thing is printed at once - leading to the obvious potential
problems with Wind Dance et al, but on a bigger scale. 100 extra cards
knocking around to accidentally find their way into boosters.

In the latter instance, the expansions are pumped out at a break-neck
pace. Huge expansions are playtested with no knowledge at all of what
has preceded them. How do you anticipate 300 new cards that you've
never seen when, due to the time limits, you have to have your report in
exactly when it's released. Imagine a time-scale of Bloodlines being
released in January this year and the Camarilla Edition going out in
late April/early May. For final re-edits, design, printing, testing,
distribution, publicity, you're barely going to get chance to see
Bloodlines, let alone figure out its impact on the cards you're
playtesting. ("Oh my God, look at that Temporis card! That fallback
level is exactly what we were saying the new Brujah shouldn't have
access to when we showed how broken this new card was!")

That might be a game that falls under a definition of "well supported"
that only caters to "rapid expansion release", but it could also be a
game with a poor quality control process - which wouldn't exactly be
"well supported" under a quality-oriented definition.

the release of the previous set. Sabbat War obviously did (no new cards
immediately prior to it). I know that The Camarilla Edition did.

This comes under the problem that was mentioned previously:

And try to identify any card games *outside* of the obvious
Hasbro/Wizards set that release at least every six months that
have any longevity. I'd struggle to name many.

What applies to other games simply isn't feasible to other, smaller
games. Every six months? Every four months? The designers don't even
necessarily know what's in Bloodlines, because it hasn't been sent to
press and is still in playtesting, and they're already having to design
The Camarilla Edition. They don't know how grouping has faired under
playtesting, but they're already having to design (potentially) Group 3
Gangrel.

Sure, if your game is going to sell millions of cards and you can count
on profit margins that will allow for a full time school of playtesters,
designers, artists, web designers, customer liaisons and so on, you can
generate things a lot faster, more reliably, more stably and so on.
There's also the fact that someone like Hasbro could afford full/part-
time playtesters as a matter of course because they have sufficient card
games that they'd never be idle. You spend a few weeks testing the new
Harry Potter expansion to oblivion, then while the designers are
reworking it, you get them working on some Magic re-writes for the next
DCI errata list.

But with games that are orders of magnitudes smaller, that's simply
unfeasible.

It is also useful to examine what Wizards of the Coast have managed with
a rapid production schedule in the past. Certainly, many broken cards
have been generated, many concepts tested insufficiently. The number
under a slower schedule, per White Wolf? There have been a number of
cards where people have gone "Ugh, I don't like that" - Meddling of
Semsith is a classic example. Some people just don't like the mechanic.
Not a lot you can do about that. But the number of power rares? The
number of must have cards? The number of times something like
Necropotence dominance has been forced onto the V:TES scene? Bear in
mind that WotC managed Thoughts Betrayed, Tomb of Rameses III, Return to
Innocence and so forth under their system.

Is a game that generates b0rked cards from a design team acting rapidly
useful under terms such as "well supported"? It's rapidly supported,
but "well" tends to imply some measure of quality. If they're to do
something "well", it coming out good in the end is useful.

So rapid expansion certainly has an interesting track record. The
history suggests that doing things "well" isn't always what happens.

>> As far as I can recall, each set so far has had at least some not
>> insignificant portion of the proofing and playtesting take place after
>> the release of the previous set. Sabbat War obviously did (no new cards
>> immediately prior to it). I know that The Camarilla Edition did.
>
>Not for the set I playtested.

It's worth pointing out that not all playtesting will, of necessity,
always involve all persons at all times, with all cards. Some
playtesters may well also come across from previous playtesting, whilst
others will not, who will have different knowledge levels. Such
diversity of timing and people can provide multiple different view-
points, reflecting different styles and so forth. One important point
is that the designers can also be playtesting concepts themselves,
amongst themselves and their playgroups, which also facilitates
different views.

Nor does it seem terribly likely that no playtester, including
designers, thought of decks focused on Tyler. That the card exists in
the game in a usable form doesn't mean it wasn't thought of. Perhaps it
was demonstrated to be balanced. Perhaps it wasn't demonstrated to be
problematic to a level the Design Team thought to be problematic.
Perhaps it was thought of, but the relevant playtester didn't write it
up sufficiently, or at all. Whatever.

Tyler is certainly a good vampire, asking to be used for *something*.
And with those disciplines (Fortitude complimenting the multiple
actions, for instance), a powerful vampire. Leaving the specials to one
side, that's 9 points of disciplines, and 9 points of pretty good
disciplines. Reasonable co-operation, ugh, synergy. "dom" provides a
useful piece of co-operation with the Euro-Brujah, for instance. For
and Obf aren't bad at all, For for the extra, extra untaps. Primogen,
not bad, but on a 9 capacity vampire, it's not a Prince or Justicar.
Good enough? If you're going for a focused Tyler deck, you're missing
out on Fifth Tradition, Second Tradition and so on - useful cards all.

The +1 bleed or additional vote is excellent, but costed. So, it's
certainly not 1.5 points for the bleed, and a vote is considered to be
0.5 points, and we're not going to the level of Prince (the extra useful
cards). A vampire with the text Primogen, casts 2 votes (instead of
one), wouldn't *really* be worth the whole 1 point of a Prince, would
it? So you run off into a few things like Command of the Harpies as a
Prince (Primogens get Beyond Reproach as a downside), it's generally not
going to be as good as a Praxis to yourself. So that can't really be
half a point (Primogen->Prince = 0.5 point), and with the cost on the +1
bleed, that goes down to, say, a point. 1 + 0.25 (vote) + 0.25
(increased flexibility) goes to 1.5, say.

9 points, + 1.5 + 0.5 = 11

Then there's the diablerie special. Now, Tyler, primogen. The Primogen
contributes to avoiding a Blood Hunt, as can the extra vote special.
But you still have to get someone in torpor first, so you can use
Amaranth or commit diablerie. Now, that's not impossible, of course -
but you're using a big vampire like Tyler. You need multiple actions,
and a rush action may be blocked (so you can't use Freak Drive). So you
need to pull off the Amaranth in combat to guarantee that. Without
extra actions, you're at a capacity deficit - the weenie decks can push
four actions a turn through, you get one. And if you are going for the
multiple untap, Amaranth special, you have to be careful about defending
Tyler too. It's such a pain trying to craft multiple action generation,
torporisation (rush + combat), a good flow of Amaranth *and* the defence
against the Blood Hunts. A good political deck on the table screws you,
if you can't survive the Blood Hunts. And a canny political deck is
going to be worried about you. You have a lot of combat savvy, which is
going to whittle him down.

Or you get several people on the table with a few votes. You've spent 9
points on a Primogen, so you're not exactly swimming in pool. None of
the obvious Princes have any stealth, so Fifth Tradition is difficult
with them. (Jaroslav, Justicar, so the same benefits - 2nd, 5th, etc. -
has Obf at 10 capacity.) Minion Tap/Taste of Vitae is a good, and well
documented, alternative avenue. But you still have the action deficit,
even with a greater pool flow, and more delicate problems with card
flow.

And a bloody big target sign on Tyler's head if you *do* pull it off.

Not a lot for the playtesters to spot, really. If Tyler looked a lot
different in playtest, it got caught well, and the resulting vampire is
really rather well balanced. The blood and untap come from a really
risky situation of diablerie - certainly something that happens
infrequently in most games I've seen, unless/until someone has real vote
dominance. I couldn't put it at more than a point, which leaves my
costing at 12 points max, and probably less than that. 11.5 say. And
for a vampire who's supposed to be 11 points ish (9+2), that works out
not badly, I'd say, given that the line for exploitation is a tricky
one.

>Why didn't you block the Archon vote?

>
>Tyler (9-cap)

Well, that's not entirely necessary. Other options involving combat
could be used. Of course, Rowan Ring is a good option.

It's also notable that use of Rowan Ring runs counter to obvious Brujah
pro-combat strategies. To avoid Majesty and Strike: Combat Ends in
general, Dodge and various scary fight back scenarios, you use IG - you
can't Breath of the Dragon under Immortal, for instance.

Obviously, there are a few steal/destroy equipment cards, but most of
them can be ignored for now - they're usually not worth the card slots,
so you can't really suggest them as a useful option for decks, though
Anarch Troublemaker could be of use. Most of the anti-equipment cards
aren't that great usually, though. Things change, of course, and
various pro-equipment strategies could make them a lot more playable.

Fat Al's does have its advantages here - but that can get burned, too.

>Prince or Justicar (minimum 5-cap)

Or another vote. Tyler could make herself a Prince if you were really
desperate. I'd probably include one or two PSes just in case.

It's also worth noting that if you *do* use a real Prince, or one who's
been around for a turn or two (say, you call Brujah Justicar on a small
vampire whilst you're getting Tyler out), the moment Tyler comes out
(Influence phase) there's a whole turn around the table for people to
say "Bugger" and run for cover/attempt to take one of them out.

>That P/J to call the Archon vote
>That P/J to pass the Archon vote

Obvious strategy here isn't blocking the vote, though that definitely
works, but to cancel it. Delaying Tactics is excellent, providing
another turn around the table to attack the vampire or whatever counter
strategy you see fit.

If a deck can't take out a key voting vampire, can't defend against
votes (intercept), can't defend against votes (counter votes/vote
cancellation) or similar, it's going to get screwed by a voting deck -
at which point, it becomes its own fault anyway.

>The deck to not get the Archon immediately voted away

Well, this is ever so slightly less true.

If you put two vampires out at once, and the other vampires calls the
Archon, it could be called first. Of course, if you get screwed by card
flow, you can find yourself without anything/much to do, and you have to
go round the table, and the Archon can be got rid of then.

>Opposing combat decks that cannot kill Tyler

This is the general problem for the Brujah. They're much better at
taking out non-combat/low-combat decks than others, but they're pretty
bad at taking it from other combat decks.

Well, this is the problem. You can be screwed by multiple different
combat strategies. Not that all of them will necessarily kill you, of
course, but they'll be doing things you can't predict.

Counter-maneuvers is the popular 'good player' move against combat decks
- particularly the Brujah. The combo now needs Archon rush, secure
close range, don't get dodged/S:CE-ed. Of course, Psyche! is always an
option - but if you're having to secure close range, it's a harder one,
because you now need this *and* this.

if you end up in combat - so Freak Drive isn't playable, so you *have*
to get the diablerie.

If anti-equipment combat is on the rise - which it mostly should be -
you then have that problem, too.

single vote push (Bewitching, say) and Rowan Ring, you have four cards,

(three discards on the three turns to get Tyler out, assuming no speed
ups - but then the speed up gets you to about ten cards), that's
approximately three tenths of the deck being Freak Drive. Say 25% with
a lucky draw. That's still, what, 22 cards. Even at 20%, that's 18
cards.

Amaranth? That's a lot of cards to get rid of.

Additionally, unlike a (picking a random deck archtype) generic Brujah
combat deck with a large combo, you need all the pieces here in pretty
much the right order. Brujah combat can cope without an Undead
Strength, maybe pulling one after it plays the Blur and putting in on
additional strikes. Ventrue votes can cope without Kindred Restructure
now, and Kine Resources instead. On such decks, Direct Intervention
isn't that good an option - Boohoohoo, I didn't play Bum's Rush, I'll
play Computer Hacking instead. This deck is more vulnerable to single
card targeting with DI, significantly so, I'd say.

>> If a deck can't take out a key voting vampire, can't defend against
>> votes (intercept), can't defend against votes (counter votes/vote
>> cancellation) or similar, it's going to get screwed by a voting deck -
>> at which point, it becomes its own fault anyway.

>Against "normal" vote decks, though, you have the whole game to
>defend - you don't have to have it This Turn Or You're Done.

DEI!!! All decks get lucky breaks and sweep tables, so perfect
scenarios are slightly less relevant - unless the perfect scenario can
be easily achieved.

You need a Prince or a Justicar. That's an investment in a Praxis
Seizure/Brujah Justicar. That's an investment in Will of the Council.
That's an investment in another vampire. In the first two instances,
that's an action to block. In the third, that's a vampire to target
*and* a delay on Tyler.

In the third instance, the idea that you can just rely on Tyler isn't an
option. You need that Prince out to call the Archon. The rush deck on
the table is going to hit Volker as hard as it damn well can, Tyler's
Fortitude be damned. (And if you're playing Flash/Rowan Ring/Blur
(anti-Dodge)/Psyche! as your major combat cards, Volker can't do
anything too flash.)

Brujah are not stealth monsters. +1 stealth is all they can expect, +2
with Alacrity. (Alas, none of these actions are bleed actions, so
Carthage Remembered is not an option.) In the instance of a vote, you
need to pass the vote. How are you doing this? Vote push? More tech.
(Though Oxford University (*spit*), England is potentially a good
option.) If you're not using vote push tech, how are you passing
Archon? True, you have a Prince (however you've done it, eventually)
and so have the options of Closed Session but, even so, not fun.

Additionally, compare having two vampires out bleeding heavily.
Laptop/Freak/Govern the Unaligned/Command of the Beast/Conditioning,
twice. 1 + 1 (laptop) + 2 (Govern) + 1 (CotB) + 3 (Conditioning). The
Laptop is at +1 stealth, just like the vote or Will of the Council. If
we can say that Will of the Council/PS/BruJus gets through due to lack
of intercept, we can say the same about the equip, right? And since
we're not throwing a vote push, let's stick Lost in Crowds in there.
DOM/For/Obf with Catherine du Bois, 5 cap. If you're happy going with
Dom/For/Obt (switch your stealth modifier over), you've got Gerard,
Aurora and Kassiyim at 5 and 6 cap. Only 7 bleed. Stick a Pentex (tm)
Loves You in, maybe. If you can guarantee as smooth a ride of Freak
Drives as the Tyler deck, you've even got some blockers free at the end.
And you're bringing out a five and a six. With Tyler plus a Fortitude
weenie (your idea, below) or Tyler plus a Prince (e.g. Volker), you're
still level in terms of transfers - Zillah's Valley could make a
difference, due to your mid-range capacity.

Of course, somehow, you get Will of the Council, Archon, a vote push,
Rowan Ring and three Freak Drives in hand (not necessarily all at once)
without getting choked by the Psyche! and Amaranth you're putting in.
If you want to be consistently pulling those, and you're not going to be
playing many cards per combat, how many have you got in? And how many
of those aren't sitting in your hand now? We're down to, say, 15 cards,
and we've got the 7 above. By your alternative scenarios, you've got a
couple of Daring the Dawn, too. Where's the Amaranth? And what are you
doing with it when it's preventing your combo from going off?

>>

>
>Yeah, this shouldn't be an issue most of the time, since presumably
>Tyler's first rampage will be to eat all the opposing voters.

Well, additionally, if you're packing sufficient Archon to pull one
sufficiently early, you'll be able to call it again.

>> >Opposing combat decks that cannot kill Tyler
>>

>Again, Tyler is much better than "the Brujah" at taking it.

It does rather depend on how directly you construct the deck.

If you're using additional vampires to call/pass the vote, they need to
survive too. If you're not, you're eating up your library with copies
of Bewitching Oration to get a fighting chance of passing it. A 9 cap
vampire having three votes from PS/Will of the Council+special (maybe
four, if you bleed/freak drive in the middle of the combo to get the
edge) trying to pass a critical political action card, so 4 (5) votes in
play, is going to find some opposition to itself quickly. 4 votes at
that point? It's certainly findable.

Indeed, voting strategies have been gradually empowered over a few sets
- Free States Rant, Baltimore Purge and so on are good votes. So you're
missing intercept for the actions, you're missing specific vote defence,
you're missing combat defence, you're missing anti-equipment cards.
What is the deck or, indeed, any deck on the table defending itself
with? And Tyler has been out a turn, you've had a turn of play. Empty
your hand, no matter how stupidly, draw into your defence.

>If all else fails, you could Daring the Dawn with Tyler on the
>"equip Rowan Ring" action, rescue with a Fortitude weenie +
>Daring the Dawn, and then your opponents are no longer in a
>"just block Tyler" situation.

What about the Will of the Council and the Archon? Sure, you can get
round some problems. But if you get out Will of the Council *and* the
Archon by using Daring the Dawn, you're going very slowly.

And again, we've got a hand of seven cards and we're, let's say, 15
cards in. 2 copies of Daring the Dawn? That's 12 per deck (or similar
style tech, Day Operation etc.). Along with some of the Freak Drives
from earlier, we're taking up a lot of the deck with Fortitude action
modifiers.

Here again, Direct Intervention is a good option. If you throw it on
Daring the Dawn, they can't repeat that - the action modifier has been
played, just to no effect. And DI isn't an uncommon card to find thrown
around in a game, it's just this deck is so vulnerable to card flow.

>> In message <avcklo$e2i73$1...@ID-121616.news.dfncis.de>, Joshua Duffin

>
>> >I don't think Brujah combat is really relevant here. Only
>> >Tyler is important. She can deal with Breath of the Dragon

>> >Psyche against S:CE instead of Grappling.
>>
>> Well, this is the problem. You can be screwed by multiple different
>> combat strategies. Not that all of them will necessarily kill you, of
>> course, but they'll be doing things you can't predict.
>
>Yes. There's always a counter to every deck. Whether it's something
>that fits into decks that are actually tournament worthy themselves,
>or likely to show up in tournaments, isn't as certain...

Well, Strike: Combat Ends is still pretty tournament worthy. Guns are
showing up more and more, as we both note. Both are viable forms of
combat defence, and both are fairly popular. (S:CE is not a no-brainer,
as in years gone by, but it is still certainly viable.)

Other pro-combat decks turn up a fair bit, and are often seen in finals
of tournaments, from the reports I read.

It would be an unusual, or very un/lucky, tournament where at least a
couple of strong pro-combat decks weren't around, I'd've thought.

>> Counter-maneuvers is the popular 'good player' move against combat decks
>> - particularly the Brujah. The combo now needs Archon rush, secure
>> close range, don't get dodged/S:CE-ed. Of course, Psyche! is always an
>> option - but if you're having to secure close range, it's a harder one,
>> because you now need this *and* this.
>
>That's why it's good that Rowan Ring/Amaranth reduces the *necessary*
>part of the combat combo so much: it leaves you a lot of room for
>things like Psyche and Pursuit (probably the best anti-go-to-long
>option for Tyler since it can also be used for anti-Dodge and is very
>easily tossable if necessary (strike hands, Pursuit, Rowan Ring)).

It's less certain that that. You need to get the Rowan Ring in hand,
and you need to get it out. It's the general problem of uniques
clogging up a deck. To get one in hand early, you're probably going to
want 6 or 7 in a deck. Even with a couple of Fat Al's, you're locking
up deck space for it. Along with the Will of the Council (again, half a
dozen copies) and the Archon (again, have a dozen copies), in a 90 card
deck, you'll have 6 of these turning up in your first thirty cards.
Along with the Freak Drives, to make it a one turn scenario, you'll
need, say, 18 Freak Drive in the deck (going for the low end of the
maths previously). Another 6 in the first 30. You need some vote push
tech. Again, to draw early, you need several. Let's say 4 Bewitching
Oration (or similar) and 2 Oxford University. Another 2.

That's 2 Rowan Ring, maybe 1 Fat Al's, 2 Will of the Council, 2 Archon,
6 Freak Drive, 2 Bewitching Oration/Oxford University. 15 cards so far.
The other 15 could be pro-combat and/or defence. But at the same time
as you're playing those, you're continually drawing into repeats of the
action cards you've just played.

You can't play the Rowan Rings (contest), you can't play the Will of the
Council (no more Primogen), you could play the Archon I guess which
would allow the Bewitching Oration. Maybe there's an Elysium: The
Arboretum on hand to burn and use the Bewitching Oration. But it's
starting to clog.

Now, you can go down to smaller numbers, of course, and try to cycle
more. But until you can get those cards, you haven't really got the
killer combo off.

And if we're down to taking the actions over several turns, because the
Freak Drives aren't turning up, then the One Turn or DEI premonitions
aren't relevant - it's not happening in one turn.

>> Intercept is also a good option here. The action doesn't succeed - even
>> if you end up in combat - so Freak Drive isn't playable, so you *have*
>> to get the diablerie.
>
>Sure. There should be a lot of Amaranth in the deck though,

How much? And how much is going to push the Will of the Council/Rowan
Ring/Archon/Freak Drive pieces out of hand?

>and each
>time an Amaranth goes off, you have one less person who can try to
>block things...

Again, you do need the Amaranth to go off, though. Decks without combat
defence are always going to get screwed by combat, that's simply a
given. And decks with combat in them are almost certain to turn up in a
tournament.

>> I don't think the combos can be easily brought down to Rowan
>> Ring/Amaranth.
>
>No, what I'm saying is, that's all you *have* to have, once you have
>the Rowan Ring, is an Amaranth. This is orders of magnitude less
>card-intensive for its nastiness in combat than "traditional" Brujah
>combat using, say, Torn Signpost, Immortal Grapple, Undead Strength,
>Taste of Vitae.

That's true, but, unlike many permanent vs transient situations, you
can't cycle these out - and you have to take an action.

In the first instance, of transient card intensity, we can break a
Brujah combat deck down to Bum's Rush, Flash, Torn Signpost, Immortal
Grapple, Undead Strength, Taste of Vitae - with a few Computer Hackings,
a few Minion Taps/Blood Dolls (depending on the deck) and a small clutch
of Haven Uncovered. What happens when our card flow sucks? I draw
Bum's Rush, a Torn Signpost and a Taste of Vitae, and happen to have
Computer Hacking, another Bum's Rush, Haven Uncovered and maybe a
Potence master. But I can still play my cards - Bum's Rush is fine.
Torn Signpost is fine. I can have a go with Taste of Vitae, though it
might not do much. And I'll draw into some more cards.

In the instance of other permanent cards, we might be playing .44
Magnum. These have the advantage of not needing Fortitude to bring out
(they're available with Concealed Weapon), so we can play with multiple
vampires and none of them are so key. I can play multiples, cycling to
avoid hand sticking, which Rowan Ring can't.

If we're going for single vampire Tyler, we can't play multiple Will of
the Council. If we're not going for SVT, the obvious companions are a
Prince (who couldn't play WotC, at which point you might not be putting
it in the deck but then expose yourself to other problems) or a weenie
for the scenarios you suggest. Can't cycle there. It's not actually
Unique (other people can play it), but to most intents and purposes,
it'll conflict with itself in your deck just as much as Rowan Ring. Two
cards that are just going to eat discards. *And* you're vulnerable to
card flow. As a transient combat deck, a Bum's Rush or a blocked action
is fine by me, and there are a few useful built in rush vampires (mostly
ignorable, however). You don't *need* Flash before Undead Strength is
playable. You don't *need* Torn Signpost before Taste of Vitae is
playable. Sure, you might have to cycle uselessly to get to your cards,
but they can all work on their own.

Rowan Ring is playable at any point in the combo. But Will of the
Council is needed *before* Archon - no blocked actions for me. You need
Archon and some vote tech if you're going to guarantee it - but at the
same time, you need little enough that they don't stuff your hand full.
And you can't easily cope with Will of the Council, Archon, Bewitching
Oration, Amaranth, Amaranth, Rowan Ring, Psyche! in hand. No freak
drives, no Single Turn Or DEI.

>> >Or, for super-tech action, Tyler does: Will of the Council, Freak
>> >Drive, Archon herself. Freak Drive, Rowan Ring, Freak Drive, go to
>> >town. Best-case scenario, of course.
>>

<snip - my problems>

>
>All true. But see where I said "best case scenario"? That's not
>something I'd *expect* to happen, it's just *possible*. :-)

But that's the trick. This is the best case action for a Tyler deck
going for a single Tyler. (Not relying on Volker to call an action
etc.)

The best case scenario is *very* tricky to pull off.

And if the problem is, as you say, that:

"Against "normal" vote decks, though, you have the whole game to
defend - you don't have to have it This Turn Or You're Done."

then it's not a single turn. And you have the whole set-up time to
defend against it.

And against "normal" vote decks, you could be in a similar position.
Three turns, say, to bring out a couple of vampires. Maybe four.
(Three turns minimum for Tyler, with no transfer tech.) They pull a
Ventrue Headquarters, a Directorate Assembly or similar. You've done
similar. You're at, what, 15, 16 pool, maybe, if you've gone for
another vampire too. But in any case, two Parity Shifts could do a lot
of damage. If you go for weenie-ish voters with Presence push, you
could get hit with 3, 4, 5 KRCs.

Now, in this single turn of death, you can only defend with intercept or
anti-vote. Against the Tyler deck, you've had a previous turn at least
where Tyler was the obvious vampire to take on - multiple vampire decks
can "afford" to lose one or two, in that they won't just flollop as a
result. You can intercept any of the actions (or you're going for nasty
Daring the Dawn situations). You can vote down the vote. You can
cancel the vote. You can block the combat. You can block the
equipment. You can defend in the combat. You can fight back in the
combat (can't Amaranth if you're going to torpor).

There are many defences available in the game. The most generic action
wise is intercept. Specifically, you can get anti-vote (Delaying
Tactics, vote cancellers, vote gainers) and anti-bleed (bounce,
reduction etc.) In combat, you can get combat defence, or outside
combat you could try Obedience (not good against Tyler).

So you haven't got any intercept - general action defence. The vote has
got through, so you haven't got any vote defence. The combat happens,
and you haven't got any combat defence. The only major defence you
haven't had a chance to use is bleed defence.

You've had a similar amount of time to attack the vampires - and he only
has one vampire to take out.

So, in one turn, you need intercept (multiple times), or combat, or vote
defence. Against the weenie voters, you need intercept or vote defence,
nothing else will work - but other sources work against Tyler (pro-
combat, anti-combat, anti-equipment for instance). Yet that can be just
as One Turn Or DEI. And the Tyler deck may well have been going over
several turns, not one, because of the Freak Drives.

>> Additionally, unlike a (picking a random deck archtype) generic Brujah
>> combat deck with a large combo, you need all the pieces here in pretty
>> much the right order. Brujah combat can cope without an Undead
>> Strength, maybe pulling one after it plays the Blur and putting in on
>> additional strikes. Ventrue votes can cope without Kindred Restructure
>> now, and Kine Resources instead. On such decks, Direct Intervention
>> isn't that good an option - Boohoohoo, I didn't play Bum's Rush, I'll
>> play Computer Hacking instead. This deck is more vulnerable to single
>> card targeting with DI, significantly so, I'd say.
>
>In actual play, probably not that much. You're going to have plenty
>of copies of Archon and Amaranth just to be able to draw them enough,

Plentiful copies of Archon isn't always a good thing. Where/how do you
ditch them?

>and either plenty of Rowan Ring or Vast Wealths for them (Vast Wealthed
>Rowan Ring isn't DIable).

Yes, one of the fun bits of Vast Wealth. :)

To get out Vast Wealth, you also need plentiful copies of that.
Competes for Master slots, and if you're going for Minion Tap as pool
gain...

>Yeah, when people foil you with some method (eg blocking the equip)
>and you use Neet Tech to counter-foil them, your counter-foil is
>vulnerable to DI. But people won't even try to foil you all the
>time, and how many DI can they realistically pack? Not that many.

No, true. I wouldn't posit DI as a counter defence to all systems. But
a number of decks pack a few as a "If something nasty happens, I
have..." sort of defence. Against many decks, it is definitely as you
suggest.

Play it on the Freak Drive in the middle of the set-up and the action
modifier has been played and *it doesn't matter* if they have another
one. It's been played on that action.

http://groups.google.com/groups?selm=3CF28DC8.7F0482B1%40white-wolf.com

>> I'm still unsure that it's ever going to consistently be One Turn Or
>> DEI!!! All decks get lucky breaks and sweep tables, so perfect
>> scenarios are slightly less relevant - unless the perfect scenario can
>> be easily achieved.
>
>Sure. But this one, if you get the Archon and Rowan Ring on, the next
>turn Tyler may be able to eat as many vampires as she has Amaranths
>for. With no more cards played. That's the turn on which it becomes
>Have The Defense Now Or Cry.

No, that's the turn on which it becomes "Have Some Defence Of One Of
Several Types For The Past Three Turns Or So or DEI." Tyler comes out,
whole turn to take action against her. Will of the Council, Freak
Drive, Archon. Lots of options there. Whole turn to take action
against her. Rowan Ring comes out (some options here). Maybe we Freak
here, and let Archon go off. Lots of combat options. If you're still
dying, you've had three turns to do something about it.

I'm not sure how that's significantly different to many decks. I bleed
you, I bleed you, I bleed you. My Lasombra or Malkavian example is
using similarly intense amount of cards, each of which it can reuse when
it draws them - unlike the use this deck has for excess Rowan Ring and
Will of the Council. And if we have three turns to bleed, that's 21
bleed.

Now, if you say "But I could intercept or bounce or...", well, what's
the problem with having defence (or pro-active take out actions) against
the Tyler deck?

And since it's three turns to bring out Tyler, a faster deck can already
do significant damage to the deck - with votes (oops, is that a problem
for passing Archon?), with bleed (no vampires to defend? shame), with a
pro-active rush immediately (oh, you've got Rowan Ring and Amaranth in
your hand, what a pity), with a Pentex Subversion (this seemed to go
through a renaissance a couple of years ago, and then die) or any other
card suitable for single vampire scariness.

>> In the third instance, the idea that you can just rely on Tyler isn't an
>> option. You need that Prince out to call the Archon. The rush deck on
>> the table is going to hit Volker as hard as it damn well can, Tyler's
>> Fortitude be damned. (And if you're playing Flash/Rowan Ring/Blur
>> (anti-Dodge)/Psyche! as your major combat cards, Volker can't do
>> anything too flash.)
>
>What rush deck on the table? Have you seen the EC results? ;-)

(Joke noted, but addressing the point seriously, too.)

Metagames always shift to compensate for new deck styles. Any
unaccounted for deck type will do well in a virgin area. If the area
has shifted towards uber-Free States Rant/Baltimore Purge politics and
no combat, a strong combat deck will of course do well.

Combat is a perfect playable archetype, and it doesn't have to be solely
combat. Bruise and bleed is a valid archetype, for instance, and I've
long noted that having a rush or five in a bruise and bleed deck is an
excellent option.

That some areas get skewed into situations that perfectly valid and
playable and well-used (elsewhere) decks don't occur isn't a wonderfully
valid argument for action. The obvious example of such in the past is
any xCL argument that revolves around "We do it to make bleed less
powerful" and, similarly, "Ban this card because I can't stop it."

I'd much prefer to see Tyler's strengths seriously tested before any
real action is taken.

>> In the first two, you have some problems. As Derek Ray points out, the
>> Brujah are not stealth monsters. +1 stealth is all they can expect, +2
>> with Alacrity. (Alas, none of these actions are bleed actions, so
>> Carthage Remembered is not an option.) In the instance of a vote, you
>> need to pass the vote. How are you doing this? Vote push? More tech.
>> (Though Oxford University (*spit*), England is potentially a good
>> option.) If you're not using vote push tech, how are you passing
>> Archon? True, you have a Prince (however you've done it, eventually)
>> and so have the options of Closed Session but, even so, not fun.
>
>What intercept? Have you seen the EC results? ;-)

So people are only playing stealth and bleed and get screwed by a deck
that effortlessly exploits the holes in stealth and bleed.

Sux2bethem.

Bear in mind that, of the combat/vote/bleed triumvirate, we've just
wiped out combat, we've wiped out intercept as a by-line and that any
political decks on the table stand a good chance of trouncing the Archon
vote. So this environment has to be only bleed or screwball.

It may be surprising, but I don't believe in balancing decks or cards
because of an environment where only bleed and screwball decks are
played.

>Look. I know this isn't the end-all and be-all of vampire deck tech.
>Nothing is, or ever can be, since DI and Sudden Reversal exist. All
>I'm saying is, it's probably real nasty, and not every environment is
>going to consistently have the things that foil it at the right time,

The same can be said of *any* good deck. This environment might have no
bleed bounce and so I screw everyone with my super stealth and bleed
deck.

>and because of the way it operates, if you don't have it at the right
>time you might as well not have it at all.

But unless the deck is on a stupid streak of luck (by your own
admission), you've had multiple turns.

If your deck has defence that you can't access when you have warning,
you've either had a supremely had shuffle (all decks have that) or
you've made a deck that can't access its defence. What are you going to
do when my 3 dom weenies bleed you for 4 each? And next turn?

>> Of course, somehow, you get Will of the Council, Archon, a vote push,
>> Rowan Ring and three Freak Drives in hand (not necessarily all at once)
>> without getting choked by the Psyche! and Amaranth you're putting in.
>> If you want to be consistently pulling those, and you're not going to be
>> playing many cards per combat, how many have you got in? And how many
>> of those aren't sitting in your hand now? We're down to, say, 15 cards,
>> and we've got the 7 above. By your alternative scenarios, you've got a
>> couple of Daring the Dawn, too. Where's the Amaranth? And what are you
>> doing with it when it's preventing your combo from going off?
>
>The deck probably doesn't have to be, and probably usually won't be,
>a Super-Turbo-Tyler-Killz-All deck.

At which point, what's the problem?

>It can more realistically use
>a "voting Brujah" module as support,

Which provides many avenues for exploitation by opposing players. *And*
any cards you do put in for Tyler's benefit (Fortitude, primarily)
aren't hugely playable by that module. (No Princes with Fortitude for
the Brujah. 10 cap Justicar.)

And if you're now putting less Fortitude in, how does Tyler defend
himself against fight back? Hit me, I hit back, both go to torpor and,
hmm, nice here, isn't it?

>and "only" eat a bunch of
>opposing vampires when the right cards eventually show up.

Erm, isn't that precisely what any combat deck does? And usually with a
little more regularity.

>> >If all else fails, you could Daring the Dawn with Tyler on the
>> >"equip Rowan Ring" action, rescue with a Fortitude weenie +
>> >Daring the Dawn, and then your opponents are no longer in a
>> >"just block Tyler" situation.
>>
>> What about the Will of the Council and the Archon? Sure, you can get
>> round some problems. But if you get out Will of the Council *and* the
>> Archon by using Daring the Dawn, you're going very slowly.
>
>No, see, in this "all else fails" scenario, you'd be getting the
>Rowan Ring first, and then people can't cavalierly block your
>Will or Archon actions, cause Tyler has a Rowan Ring.

They don't need to be cavalier.

If a single piece of equipment can completely flummox a deck's ability
to defend, hasn't something gone rather wrong? And wouldn't it be
somewhat better to 'cavalier'ly sacrifice a blocker now, than have all
your vampires eaten later? It might be just me but 1 dead vampire vs
lots of dead vampires strikes me as the better option.

And in the end, if you do die, you lose all your vampires anyway. It's
unlikely to make the situation any worse.

In message <avhnfr$fjc1o$1...@ID-121616.news.dfncis.de>, Joshua Duffin

<jtdu...@yahoo.com> writes:
>Well of course. I'm not suggesting banning Tyler or anything
>like that. I'm just saying, her with Rowan Ring plus Archon
>really is a really nasty combo with repeat-Archon-rush, and
>I don't think it's as easily dismissable with "well any strong
>deck can do things that nasty" as you do.

But isn't that what makes strong decks strong? The Malkavian Madness
Network deck can do similar nastiness, out of turn, for instance.

Indeed, if you take Dave's run through of what went wrong for him, he
does point out the utility of Vast Wealth - another go round the table
next time, and it's there. Now, of course, you can't easily get rid of
Vast Wealth, but it does tend to point to a situation where players
simply aren't capitalising on the time they have. Strong combos are
hideous - but only if you give them the time.

Similarly, you can point to the fact that he was getting Rake and Volker
and Brachah and Tyler out, and there were no votes on the table - and he
was allowed that much pool gain (that's 25 pool of vampires, I think).
The other decks really should be packing vote defence - and vote defence
has the extra advantage that the political action card goes away. (Save
for the likes of Reinforcements, or Waste Management etc., which isn't
terribly significant here.) On a table with no other votes, of course a
deck with voting angles is going to have a free ride, at least with
those aspects of the deck.

Vote deck winning on table without vote defence unshocker.

Additionally, if your grand-predator is completely tying up your
predator, it's up to the predator to a) get him to back off, b) show him
why, c) explain that you need to take out the deck or it'll roll the
table (this may be a lie, but can be convincingly backed up), d) other
forms of diplomacy.

The Tyler deck archetype is undoubtedly powerful, if played well and
with, of course, the addition of a little luck (which we all need). And
with good players behind flexible, powerful decks, they'll do well. But
if the rest of the table isn't including votes or vote defence, and your
predator and grand-predator are fighting amongst themselves without
putting any pressure on you (which may occur via subtle diplomacy,
manipulation and so on), of course a deck is going to go well.
